prompt: TLS does encryption and session-key negotiation, which is OSI Presentation/Session-layer work. Where does TLS actually sit in the real TCP/IP protocol stack?
choices: As a distinct Presentation layer between the Internet layer and the Transport layer
As a shim running directly on top of TCP and directly below the application protocol (e.g. HTTP)
Inside the IP header as an optional extension
As part of the Link layer, alongside Ethernet framing

prompt: You need subnets of a /20 network that each support at least 200 hosts. How many host bits are required, and what is the resulting subnet prefix length?
choices: 7 host bits, /25 prefix
8 host bits, /24 prefix
9 host bits, /23 prefix
6 host bits, /26 prefix

prompt: A client sends a SYN with Seq=500000. The server replies with SYN,ACK carrying Seq=900000. What Ack value must the client's final ACK of the three-way handshake contain?
In a dig +trace resolution of www.example.com, the root servers respond with a referral to the .com TLD servers. What does that response NOT contain?
choices: NS records naming the .com TLD servers
Glue A records giving the IP addresses of those TLD servers
An authoritative answer (aa flag set) with www.example.com's actual IP address
Data placed in the authority/additional sections rather than the answer section

prompt: In an HTTP/1.1 request, what is the purpose of the mandatory Host header?
choices: It tells the client which TCP port to connect to
It lets a single server IP serving multiple domains (virtual hosting) know which site's content to return
It specifies the character encoding of the response body
It is required only for HTTPS, not plain HTTP

prompt: A new TCP connection starts slow start with cwnd = 10 segments and no losses occur. Roughly what is cwnd after 3 round-trip times, given that cwnd grows by one segment per ACK received?
choices: 13 segments (linear growth of ~1 per RTT)
30 segments (growth of 10 per RTT)
80 segments (roughly doubling each RTT)
10 segments (slow start does not grow cwnd until ssthresh is set)

prompt: In C socket code, why must a port number be passed through htons() before being placed into a sockaddr_in struct, when Python's socket.connect((host, port)) needs no such call?
choices: Port numbers on the wire are always sent in network (big-endian) byte order, and C exposes the raw struct fields directly, so the program must convert from the host's native byte order itself; Python's socket module performs that conversion internally
htons() is only required for IPv6 addresses, not IPv4
Python does not support TCP, only UDP, so byte order never matters
htons() converts the port number from decimal to hexadecimal for display purposes only

prompt: You capture traffic to port 443 (HTTPS) in Wireshark expecting to read the HTTP request text directly in the Follow TCP Stream view. What will you actually see, and why?
choices: The plaintext HTTP request, because TCP payloads are never encrypted at the transport layer
An encrypted TLS record layer handshake and application data, because HTTP running over port 443 is wrapped in TLS above TCP
Nothing at all, because Wireshark cannot capture any traffic on port 443
A DNS query, because port 443 is reserved for DNS over HTTPS
